## 3. Ground Truths

- **GT-1** In a blind study, GPT-4-generated submissions were injected into unsupervised, window-timed take-home exams across five undergraduate psychology modules at a UK university (Short Answer Questions: 2.5-hour window, 200-word answers; essays: 8-hour window, 1,500 words). 94% of the AI submissions went undetected by examiners (97% under stricter criteria requiring explicit mention of AI); AI submissions scored on average half a grade boundary higher than real students; there was an 83.4% chance that AI submissions on a given module would outperform a random selection of real student submissions of the same size. — source: Scarfe, Watcham, Clarke & Roesch, "A real-world test of artificial intelligence infiltration of a university examinations system: A 'Turing Test' case study," *PLOS ONE*, 2024; read-at-source: full text, PMC11206930, Results/Discussion sections (figures quoted directly).
- **GT-2** Across seven widely used AI-text detectors tested on 91 TOEFL essays written by non-native English speakers, the average false-positive rate (genuine human writing flagged as AI-generated) was 61.22%; on 88 US 8th-grade essays by native English writers, the average false-positive rate was approximately 5.19%. — source: Liang, Yuksekgonul, Mao, Wu & Zou, published in *Patterns* (2023); read-at-source: arXiv:2304.02819v3, full text, Results section (figures quoted directly).
- **GT-3** In a survey of 1,041 UK undergraduates (fielded by Savanta), 88% reported using generative AI tools for assessments in 2025 (up from 53% in 2024); 18% reported including AI-generated text directly in submitted work; 76% believed their institution would detect AI use if it occurred. — source: HEPI/Kortext Student Generative AI Survey 2025; read-at-source: hepi.ac.uk release page, 2025-02-26 (figures quoted directly).
- **GT-4** GPT-4 scored approximately 297/400 on the Uniform Bar Exam, within the 68th-90th percentile of human test-takers depending on jurisdiction and exam administration; it scored 4.2/6.0 on both the Multistate Essay Examination and the Multistate Performance Test (a score of 4+ is generally passing); it scored 75.7% on the multiple-choice component, exceeding the average human test-taker by more than 7 points. — source: Katz, Bommarito, Gao & Arredondo, "GPT-4 Passes the Bar Exam," published study; read-at-source: full text, PMC10894685 (figures quoted directly).
- **GT-5?** Retrieval-practice/testing-effect meta-analytic literature reports that information retrieved under recall/test conditions is recalled on subsequent tests roughly 2.5x more often than information reviewed via restudying, with benefits persisting over weeks to years and replicated across ages and content domains. — cited to: multiple meta-analyses summarized in web-search results (e.g., work associated with Roediger/Karpicke-line testing-effect research); reported-by-delegate: search-engine summary; cited sources not opened by this analysis.
- **GT-6?** Contract-cheating prevalence research reports self-reported contract cheating rising from a historic average of approximately 3.5% to approximately 15.7% in samples from 2014 onward; unsupervised/take-home assessment format is specifically named in this literature as expanding opportunities for collusion or outsourcing; one cited institution (UNSW) saw detected cheating rates roughly double post-COVID (approximately 2% to approximately 4.5%), coinciding with expanded remote/take-home assessment. — cited to: Newton-line meta-analytic literature, *Frontiers in Education* and related sources; reported-by-delegate: search-engine summary; cited sources not opened by this analysis.

## Trade-off analysis (process output, feeds chain C4)

## Options

- **A — Full replacement:** take-home assessment becomes the standard format; timed/invigilated exams eliminated. (This is the option the user's question names as "replace.")
- **B — Status quo:** timed, invigilated written exams remain the standard format; take-home is not adopted as a replacement.
- **C — Hybrid (composite):** a grade-load-bearing secured/timed (invigilated or live-proctored) component is retained; take-home format is used for extended/authentic tasks; an unpredictable, accommodation-inclusive, randomly sampled (~10%) oral defense (viva) is layered on take-home submissions. Conditional on design requirements A8-A13 (see Assumptions Table).

**Must-haves (knockouts):**
- M1 — must preserve the ability to certify the credential reflects the individual student's own demonstrated competence at a rate materially better than today's realistic detection capability.
- M2 — must not systematically disadvantage a protected group (non-native English speakers, disabled/anxious students) as an artifact of the chosen enforcement mechanism.
- M3 — must be operable at typical university scale (large lecture courses) without unbounded per-student cost.

**Knockout result:** Option A fails M1 — GT-1 directly measured 94% of AI submissions going undetected in exactly this format, with no auxiliary integrity mechanism specified; it also fails M2 on its own terms, since the standard fallback safeguard (AI detection) is shown by GT-2 to be biased against non-native English writers. **Option A is knocked out — not scored.** Options B and C pass all three must-haves (B trivially, as the pre-AI baseline; C conditionally, per A8-A13) and proceed to scoring.

## Criteria & Weights

| Criterion | Weight | 1 means... | 5 means... |
|---|---|---|---|
| Integrity / certification validity | 5 | >50% of graded submissions could be substantially AI-substituted with no realistic chance of detection or challenge | AI substitution is infeasible in real time, or caught/deterred at a rate high enough to make it a rational-choice-losing strategy |
| Pedagogical value / retention | 3 | format provides no retrieval-practice benefit distinct from ordinary study | format is built around closed-resource recall shown to produce durable retention gains |
| Authentic-task representativeness | 3 | format tests only closed-book recall, unlike almost any real post-graduation task | format closely mirrors resource-rich, extended real-world tasks in the field |
| Equity / accessibility (net) | 4 | format's known accessibility/fairness gaps are structural and unmitigated | format's accessibility gaps are addressed by mechanisms designed in from the outset |
| Feasibility at scale | 3 | requires ~1:1 faculty time per student with no scaling path | scales to large lecture courses with existing or lightly-augmented staffing |
| AI-resilience (2-3yr horizon) | 3 | format's integrity mechanism is already failing today and has no reason to improve | format's integrity mechanism does not depend on AI capability staying where it is today |

## Scoring

| Option | Integrity (×5) | Pedagogical (×3) | Authentic (×3) | Equity (×4) | Feasibility (×3) | AI-resilience (×3) | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| B (status quo) | 4×5=20 (GT-1 contrast case; invigilation logic) | 5×3=15 (GT-5?) | 2×3=6 (weakly-grounded normative judgment) | 2×4=8 (GT-8?) | 5×3=15 (existing pre-AI baseline) | 4×3=12 | **76** |
| C (hybrid) | 4×5=20 (C1, GT-1, GT-7; capped below 5 by A9-A11 implementation preconditions) | 4×3=12 (GT-5?, reduced frequency vs. B) | 4×3=12 (take-home component) | 4×4=16 (GT-7's built-in-accommodation condition; capped below 5 as a design requirement, not a demonstrated record) | 3×3=9 (10% sampling more scalable than full invigilation, but adds real cost; AI-assisted grading tools immature) | 4×3=12 (A13: not yet eroded, but named as time-bound) | **81** |

**Recompute check:** per-criterion (C−B) differences: Integrity 0, Pedagogical −3, Authentic +6, Equity +8, Feasibility −6, AI-resilience 0; sum = +5, matching 81−76=5 exactly.

## Recommendation

**C (hybrid) wins, 81 vs. 76, a margin of 5**, driven mainly by Equity (+8) and Authentic-task fit (+6), partly offset by Feasibility (−6) and Pedagogical value (−3).

**Flip test:** Integrity and AI-resilience are tied (0 diff) and can never flip the result by weight change alone. Authentic (max swing at weight=1: −4) and Pedagogical (max swing at weight=5: −2) cannot flip it alone within the 1-5 range. Feasibility at weight=5 (max +2 from 3) yields only a −4 swing (margin 5→1, C still wins). **Only Equity, moved from weight 4 to the floor of 1, flips the result** (contribution 8→2, a swing of −6, margin 5→−1, B wins by 1) — the single largest possible move on the criterion with the single largest weight. No other single-criterion move within the normal 1-5 range flips the winner. This is a fairly, but not overwhelmingly, robust result: it takes an extreme devaluation of Equity specifically to overturn it, and even then only by a margin of 1.

**Confidence for this collapsed chain:** capped MEDIUM — two of the six criteria (Pedagogical value, Equity) rest on `?`-marked ground truths (GT-5?, GT-8?), and the flip test shows the result's sensitivity concentrates exactly on the Equity criterion, whose factual basis (GT-8?) is unverified.

## 4. Derivation Chains

### Conclusion C1: Detector-gated take-home assessment is not a working integrity safeguard today

GT-1 (94% of AI take-home submissions undetected, real-world blind study) + GT-2 (61.22% average false-positive rate on non-native-English writing across 7 detectors)
→ even where a university requires AI-detector screening on take-home submissions as its integrity control, the tool that control relies on fails to catch the large majority of genuinely AI-written unsupervised submissions and simultaneously misflags a large share of genuine non-native-English student writing as AI-written
→ detector-gated take-home assessment is not a working safeguard, because it lets most AI-generated work through while wrongly threatening a specific subgroup of honest students — it cannot be the mechanism that makes take-home integrity-equivalent to a timed exam

**Pre-check:** head GT-1, GT-2 · ?-marked: none · lowest cited: none · Inputs ceiling: HIGH
**Confidence:** HIGH — both inputs are read-at-source with named locations, the hop is a direct combination of two independently measured figures, and the live rival ("wait for better detectors to close the gap") is settled in Abandoned Reasoning: the bias is structural (worst against the exact population screening must not falsely accuse) and detectors face purpose-built evasion tools, so nothing in this analysis supports the gap closing on the timescale a current policy decision must be made on.

### Conclusion C2: The AI-substitution problem already extends beyond take-home's current share of assessment, and is largely invisible

C1 (detector-gating doesn't work) + GT-3 (88% of surveyed students used GenAI on assessed work in 2025; 18% pasted AI text directly in)
→ the practical AI-usage rate on assessed work today is already high under current mixed timed/take-home regimes, and the one safeguard institutions lean on for take-home-specific integrity — detection — is shown non-functional by C1
→ converting the remaining timed-exam share of assessment to take-home format, with no substitute integrity mechanism, would extend the already-high and currently largely undetectable AI-substitution rate to the entire assessment portfolio, not just the take-home fraction [Assumes: A17]

**Pre-check:** head C1 (HIGH), GT-3 · ?-marked: none · lowest cited: HIGH · Inputs ceiling: HIGH
**Confidence:** MEDIUM — Inputs and the direct hop are clean, but two things keep this below HIGH: (1) the 88% figure is a weak proxy for *prohibited* substitution specifically (most of it is likely disclosed/permitted use); the tighter 18% direct-inclusion figure partially, not fully, mitigates this; (2) a live rival is not settled: GT-1's 94%-undetected finding is drawn from five psychology modules at one UK university, and generalizing it to "any university's full course portfolio," including quantitative/technical disciplines where AI text is more checkable against shown work, rests on unverified assumption A17. Verification that would remove this cause: a direct replication of GT-1's design across other disciplines and institutions.

### Conclusion C3: Timed, closed-resource recall assessment has pedagogical value that pure take-home replacement would forfeit

GT-5? (retrieval practice ~2.5x retention benefit vs. restudying)
→ the durable-retention benefit reported in this literature is produced specifically by recalling under constraint (closed-resource, time-bounded), a condition open-resource take-home work does not reproduce — take-home more closely resembles the weaker "restudying with reference" condition in the same body of research [Assumes: A14]
→ eliminating all closed-resource, time-bounded recall assessment removes a distinct pedagogical mechanism, not merely a redundant or inferior alternative to take-home work — so "take-home is strictly better pedagogy" is not supported as a blanket claim

**Pre-check:** head GT-5? · ?-marked: GT-5? · lowest cited: none · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
**Confidence:** MEDIUM — GT-5? is unverified (reported-by-delegate); the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade is locating and reading a primary meta-analysis (e.g., the Roediger/Karpicke-line testing-effect literature) directly rather than relying on a search-engine summary. Additionally, hop 1 rests on the stated premise A14 (closed-resource condition specifically drives the benefit); the chain is unaffected in direction if A14 fails narrowly, since even a weaker "assessment format affects the retention mechanism at all" reading still supports the conclusion that removing all closed-resource recall is not neutral — but the *size* of the forfeited benefit would be smaller than GT-5?'s headline figure suggests. A rival not settled here: take-home work could in principle involve genuine self-testing regardless of format, which would weaken this chain's practical import; nothing in this analysis rules that rival out.

### Conclusion C4: A hybrid model — not full replacement, not an unchanged status quo — is the recommended assessment format

GT-1 (94% AI-undetected on take-home) + GT-5? (retrieval-practice benefit) + GT-7 (sampled-viva proposal, accommodation-inclusive) + GT-8? (equity/anxiety evidence, mixed) + C1 (detector-gating doesn't work)
→ a locked, weighted trade-off across Integrity, Pedagogical value, Authentic-task fit, Equity, Feasibility, and AI-resilience gives the hybrid (Option C) a total of 81 against the pure-timed-exam status quo (Option B) at 76 — a margin of 5, driven mainly by Equity (+8) and Authentic-task fit (+6), partly offset by Feasibility (−6) and Pedagogical value (−3); full take-home replacement (Option A) was knocked out earlier on the Integrity must-have by C1 and GT-1/GT-2 directly [Assumes: A15]
→ the hybrid model is the recommended assessment format, conditional on its secured/timed component remaining genuinely grade-load-bearing and its accommodations being designed in from rollout — not the pure take-home replacement the original question named, and not an unmodified pure-timed-exam status quo either

**Pre-check:** head GT-1, GT-5?, GT-7, GT-8?, C1 (HIGH) · ?-marked: GT-5?, GT-8? · lowest cited: HIGH · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
**Confidence:** MEDIUM — capped by GT-5? and GT-8?, both unverified. Verification that would remove GT-5? as a cause: locating and reading a primary retrieval-practice meta-analysis directly (as C3 also notes). Verification that would remove GT-8? as a cause: locating and reading a primary accommodation-efficacy study directly (e.g., the Queen's University or Plymouth-hosted paper surfaced in search but not opened). The flip test recorded in the trade-off process output shows the result is sensitive specifically to the Equity criterion's weight — the one criterion resting on GT-8? — so this is the chain's named weakest link, not a generic hedge. Rival: the strongest competing conclusion is "Option B, pure timed-exam status quo, is the safer choice, since it wins if Equity is weighted down and does not depend on the hybrid's unverified implementation preconditions (A9-A13) actually holding." This rival is not fully settled — only an extreme (weight 4→1) devaluation of Equity flips the trade-off, but the implementation-precondition risk it points to is real and independently confirmed by the pre-mortem below (Clusters 1-2), which is why this chain is rated MEDIUM rather than HIGH.

### Conclusion C5: The hybrid's integrity property is durable only under specific design and resourcing conditions, and is time-bound

C4 (hybrid recommended, MEDIUM)
→[2nd] students facing unpredictable viva sampling have an incentive to shift take-home study behavior toward genuine comprehension rather than polished-but-unexamined output, partially restoring the retrieval-practice-like benefit C3 shows pure take-home would otherwise forfeit [Assumes: A16]
→[2nd] without dedicated, protected resourcing, faculty face a structural incentive to under-implement viva sampling and secured-component rigor over time, quietly reverting the hybrid toward a pure take-home model in practice even where its design is sound on paper
→[3rd] any layer of the hybrid that still leans on AI-text detectors rather than on the secured/timed component and the unpredictable viva for its integrity property remains exposed to the same detector-vendor arms race that defeats full replacement (Option A) under C1 — so the hybrid's integrity property must be designed to rest only on the load-bearing secured component and the viva, never on detection
→[3rd] over a multi-year horizon, continuing growth in AI capability documented by GT-1 and GT-4 is plausibly extended from written artifacts to real-time conversational coaching during oral defense, which would erode the viva's own integrity value on a similar timescale to how detection lost its value against written text [Assumes: A13]

**Pre-check:** head C4 (MEDIUM) · ?-marked: none · lowest cited: MEDIUM · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
**Confidence:** MEDIUM — capped by C4's own MEDIUM rating (a chain is rated no higher than the lowest-rated chain its head cites). The third-order hop on real-time AI coaching during oral defense is explicitly forward-looking: no ground truth in this analysis establishes it is occurring at scale today, so its own weight is speculative-but-foreseeable rather than established, and it is treated as a named future risk (see Falsification in the adversarial pass record) rather than a present fact.

## 5. Abandoned Reasoning

### Dead End: Rely on AI-text detectors as the primary integrity safeguard for a take-home model

**What was tried:** Considered under assumption A1/A7 — keep take-home assessment, require submissions to clear an AI-detection tool as the safeguard against undetected substitution.

**Why abandoned:** GT-2 shows detectors are both statistically unreliable and specifically biased against non-native English speakers (61.22% average false-positive rate), and detector vendors are in an active, acknowledged arms race against paraphrasing/"humanizer" tools built specifically to defeat them (Turnitin's AIR-1 deployment). The failure is structural, not a temporary lag.

**What it ruled out:** Any recommendation of the form "keep take-home, but require AI-detector clearance" as a sufficient standalone integrity mechanism (chain C1).

### Dead End: Wait for better AI detectors before changing anything

**What was tried:** Considered treating detector-improvement timelines as a legitimate basis for deferring any decision — i.e., "do nothing yet."

**Why abandoned:** This is not actually a neutral no-cost choice. GT-1 is a direct, real-world measurement of the failure mode occurring today under a format that already exists (94% undetected substitution in an unsupervised, window-timed take-home exam), so deferral leaves a known-broken safeguard running rather than avoiding a cost.

**What it ruled out:** Treating "wait for the technology to improve" as equivalent to a safe default (feeds chain C1's rival-resolution).

### Dead End: Full replacement (Option A) — take-home for everything, honor-code enforcement only

**What was tried:** Evaluated as the literal option the original question names, initially considered for full weighted scoring alongside Options B and C.

**Why abandoned:** Eliminated at the trade-off procedure's must-have knockout stage (M1: integrity) rather than scored — GT-1 is a direct, real-world measurement of exactly this failure mode, not a hypothetical concern, so scoring it alongside viable options would have let a high score on unrelated criteria out-vote a hard constraint it fails outright.

**What it ruled out:** Answering the original question as posed with a simple "yes, replace" (see trade-off process output, Options/knockout).

### Dead End: Pure timed-exam-only status quo, kept as the default because it is the incumbent

**What was tried:** Considered defaulting to "leave timed exams as the sole/dominant format, unchanged" as the presumptively safe, conservative choice.

**Why abandoned:** Scored lower than the hybrid in the locked, weighted trade-off (76 vs. 81), driven primarily by Equity and Authentic-task-representativeness; the flip test shows this result is robust to all but an extreme, hard-to-justify devaluation of the Equity criterion (chain C4).

**What it ruled out:** Treating "keep the pre-AI status quo untouched" as automatically cost-free — it is not (chain C4; GT-8?).

### Dead End: Treat retrieval-practice value (GT-5?) as dispositive on its own

**What was tried:** While building chain C3, considered recommending pure timed exams on pedagogical grounds alone, using the testing-effect literature as sufficient justification.

**Why abandoned:** Pedagogical value is only one of six locked trade-off criteria and does not by itself settle the equity and authentic-task-representativeness costs of a pure-timed-exam regime; using a single ground truth to settle a multi-criteria decision would be reasoning by a cherry-picked fact rather than the full weighted analysis the decision's stakes require.

**What it ruled out:** A single-axis "timed exams win because retention" argument (chain C3 feeds chain C4 as one of six inputs, not as a standalone verdict).

FP_EOF

## 6. Conclusion

**Recommended approach:** Do not replace timed exams outright with take-home assessments, and do not leave the pre-AI timed-exam-only status quo unchanged either — adopt a hybrid model: a grade-load-bearing secured/timed (invigilated or live-proctored) component, take-home format reserved for extended/authentic tasks, and an unpredictable, accommodation-inclusive, randomly sampled (~10%) oral defense layered on take-home submissions, with its integrity property deliberately designed to rest on the secured component and the viva rather than on AI-text detection (chain C4, chain C1).

**Key insight:** The intuitive framing of this decision as "timed exams vs. take-home" hides the fact that the safeguard most people assume would make take-home safe — AI-detection software — is not merely imperfect but measurably non-functional today, and fails worst against exactly the population (non-native English writers) it would be most damaging to wrongly accuse; a real-world blind study additionally shows the substitution problem is not hypothetical but already occurring undetected at a 94% rate in precisely this assessment format (chain C1, chain C2).

**Trade-offs acknowledged:** The hybrid model does not deliver the retrieval-practice/retention benefit of an all-timed-exam regime at full strength (chain C3, chain C4 — Pedagogical value scored 4 vs. Option B's 5), and it costs more faculty time than either pure option, with its equity and integrity benefits conditional on real resourcing and design discipline that this analysis cannot verify any specific institution will actually deliver — no chain — flagged assumption only for the institution-specific claim that resourcing will in fact be sustained, since that lies outside this analysis's evidence base (chain C5 names the resourcing and design risks generally).

**Pre-check:** head C1 (HIGH), C2 (MEDIUM), C4 (MEDIUM), C5 (MEDIUM) · ?-marked: none directly · lowest cited: MEDIUM · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
**Confidence:** MEDIUM — the recommendation rests on chain C4, itself capped MEDIUM by unverified ground truths GT-5? and GT-8?, and on chain C5, capped MEDIUM by inheriting C4's rating. Chain C1 (HIGH) and chain C2 (MEDIUM) establish the problem the recommendation responds to with higher confidence than the recommendation's own optimality; the weighted trade-off's margin (5 points) is real but not large, and the flip test shows it is sensitive specifically to the Equity criterion, whose factual basis (GT-8?) is unverified. Verification that would remove GT-5? and GT-8? as causes of the downgrade: locating and reading the primary retrieval-practice and accommodation-efficacy studies directly rather than relying on search-engine summaries.

**Would change it:** (a) a primary-source read of the retrieval-practice meta-analysis and the accommodation-efficacy literature, which could shift the Pedagogical-value and Equity scores enough to matter given the trade-off's 5-point margin (chain C4); (b) institution-specific evidence that the viva-sampling and secured-component resourcing (A9, A11) cannot be sustained, which would collapse the hybrid toward the pure take-home model the trade-off already ruled out (chain C5); (c) evidence that real-time AI coaching capable of defeating live oral defense at scale has emerged, which would erode chain C4's AI-resilience score and reopen the recommendation (chain C5).

FP_EOF

## Techniques not applied (process output)

- theoretical-limit (Phase 1 reframe invocation) — not applicable — this decision does not hinge on whether a current figure is a mere convention versus a hard physical/mathematical bound; it is a multi-criteria policy trade-off, not a limit-of-the-possible question.
- theoretical-limit (Phase 4 invocation) — not applicable — no conclusion here needs "the ceiling the fundamentals permit once conventions are stripped"; the governing constraints (AI capability, detector reliability, faculty resourcing) are empirical and institutional, not physical laws with a derivable ideal bound.
- inversion (Phase 5 adversarial-technique invocation) — not applicable — the Phase 5 conclusion (the hybrid recommendation) is a plan with actions and implementation conditions, not a bare claim; per the pre-mortem/inversion decision rule, pre-mortem is the correct tool and was applied instead (see adversarial pass record below).
- five-whys, causal mode — not applicable — no single-symptom causal-depth question was central to this analysis; the assumption space is multi-causal and was addressed by breadth (fishbone), not depth.
- five-whys, reduce-to-primitives mode — not applicable — the ground truths used are direct citations to empirical measurements/statistics (percentages, exam scores) that are already irreducible at the source, not compound claims requiring decomposition into physical or definitional primitives.
- estimate (Fermi) — not applicable — no conclusion turns on a quantity of uncertain magnitude needing unit-factor reconstruction; all quantitative figures are drawn directly from cited studies.

(fishbone was applied at Phase 2 to brainstorm the assumption space by category; inversion was applied at Phase 2 to stress-test the emerging hybrid conclusion before finalizing; trade-off was applied at Phase 4 per its structural trigger — three viable options survived the ground truths; second-order thinking was applied at Phase 4, mandatory, producing chain C5; pre-mortem was applied at Phase 5 as the adversarial technique.)

## Fishbone brainstorm (process output, feeds Phase 2 Assumptions Table)

**Effect:** What could make take-home replacement of timed exams fail to preserve valid, fair certification of individual competence?

- **People** — students differ in willingness to use AI/collude (→ A3); faculty differ in ability/willingness to detect (→ A1); some students have disabilities/anxiety poorly served by the timed format (→ A4, A8).
- **Process** — current academic-integrity processes (honor codes, detector-based hearings) predate LLM-capable writing tools (→ A1, A7); no standard viva/oral-defense process exists at most institutions yet (→ A5, A8).
- **Technology and Tools** — AI writing assistants' capability (→ A6, GT-1, GT-4); AI detectors' unreliability (→ A1, A7, GT-2); paraphrasing/"humanizer" tools built to evade detectors (→ A7); emerging voice-AI oral-exam scaling tools, currently unvalidated (→ A5).
- **Environment** — unsupervised home environment removes invigilation (→ A3, GT-6?); COVID-era shift already normalized take-home/online assessment and correlates with a rise in detected cheating (→ GT-6?).
- **Information** — students already know most peers use AI and that detection is imperfect, shifting local norms toward use (→ A3, GT-3).
- **Resources** — faculty time to design authentic/harder-to-automate assessments, or to run oral exams/vivas at scale, is scarce and unevenly available (→ A5, A11).

Each branch fed a corresponding row in the Assumptions Table (section 2) rather than being scored independently here; this scan is a coverage record, not a decision instrument in its own right.

## Inversion pass (process output, feeds Phase 2 and the pre-mortem's precondition set)

**Claim inverted:** "A hybrid assessment model preserves valid certification of individual competence while capturing take-home's authentic-task benefits" → inverted to "The hybrid model fails to preserve valid certification of individual competence."

**Failure-guaranteeing conditions enumerated:** (1) the secured/timed component's grade weight is negotiated down until it is no longer load-bearing; (2) the viva-sampling rate is predictable/self-selectable, so students route around it; (3) faculty quietly stop administering the secured component or viva sampling under time pressure; (4) viva grading is inconsistent across examiners, so it fails to discriminate genuine from AI-assisted work; (5) accommodations for the secured/timed and viva components are not resourced adequately, re-importing the status quo's equity harms while also carrying take-home's collusion risk; (6) AI capability advances to the point where real-time conversational coaching can scaffold even a live oral defense.

**Necessary preconditions derived (each a falsifiable claim, entered in the Assumptions Table as A9-A13):** A9 (secured component stays load-bearing), A10 (viva sampling stays unpredictable), A11 (institutional resourcing persists), A12 (viva grading is reliable/consistent across examiners), A13 (live AI coaching during oral defense remains preventable/detectable for the policy's expected lifespan). All five are load-bearing preconditions for the hybrid recommendation and are carried unresolved (`Accept`/`Challenge` — flagged) rather than assumed true; their failure modes directly seed the pre-mortem's five clusters below.

FP_EOF

## Adversarial pass (process output)

**Recompute.** Trade-off totals independently re-added: B = 20+15+6+8+15+12 = 76; C = 20+12+12+16+9+12 = 81. Per-criterion (C−B) differences: Integrity 5×(4−4)=0; Pedagogical 3×(4−5)=−3; Authentic 3×(4−2)=+6; Equity 4×(4−2)=+8; Feasibility 3×(3−5)=−6; AI-resilience 3×(4−4)=0. Sum of differences = −3+6+8−6+0+0 = +5, matching 81−76=5 exactly — the totals recompute cleanly. No other computed (as opposed to directly cited) figures appear in this analysis; GT-1 through GT-8's percentages and scores are quoted directly from source, not derived by this analysis's own arithmetic.

**Sensitivity.** The single ground truth whose falsity would flip chain C4's conclusion is **GT-8?** (equity/anxiety evidence): if Option B's Equity score were revised upward from 2 to 4 (i.e., if GT-8? were shown false or reversed — timed conditions carry no net anxiety disadvantage once existing accommodations are counted), the Equity contribution difference drops from +8 to 0, the margin drops from +5 to −3, and Option B wins. GT-8? is already `?`-marked, so this does not introduce a new cap — it identifies which existing `?` is doing the load-bearing work. Weakest link per chain: C1 — external validity of GT-1 (single UK university, psychology modules) generalizing broadly; C2 — the inferential gap between "88% used AI at all" and "would substitute wholesale" (A17); C3 — unverified GT-5? plus premise A14; C4 — GT-8?/the Equity criterion, as shown above; C5 — the speculative, forward-looking nature of its final hop (real-time AI coaching during oral defense), for which no ground truth in this analysis establishes current occurrence.

**Rival.** Headline conclusion (C4, hybrid recommended): strongest rival is "Option B, pure timed-exam status quo, is the safer choice, since it wins under a plausible reweighting and does not depend on the hybrid's unverified implementation preconditions (A9-A13) actually holding." This rival is not fully settled — the flip test shows it requires an extreme (4→1) devaluation of Equity to actually win, but the implementation-precondition risk it points to is real and is independently confirmed by the pre-mortem's Clusters 1 and 2 below; this is why C4 is rated MEDIUM, not HIGH, and the rival is carried live on C4's own confidence line rather than fully ruled out. Chain C1: rival "detector output could still be used as one input among several for human review, rather than discarded entirely" — rival not applicable — this is a refinement of C1's conclusion (detectors cannot be *the* safeguard), not a competing claim C1 must rule out. Chain C2: rival ("88% mostly reflects permitted use") is addressed and only partially settled on C2's own confidence line (MEDIUM), which the Rivals axis here points back to rather than re-arguing. Chain C3: rival ("take-home work can also involve genuine self-testing regardless of format") is real and unsettled, and is named directly on C3's own confidence line.

**Premise.** It is now three years since [this university] adopted the hybrid assessment model. The policy has failed — certification validity has not been restored, and the university faces a fresh integrity crisis, this time with less credibility to fix it because it already claimed to have solved the problem once.

**Causes** (unfiltered, from four viewpoints — administrator, instructor, student, rival/vendor):

*Administrator:* the secured/timed component's grade weight was negotiated down department-by-department until it was no longer load-bearing in several majors; no central budget line was created for viva administration, so it was funded out of existing TA hours that evaporated within two years; the "10% random sample" became "10% of whichever students show up to office hours," a self-selection bias defeating the design.

*Instructor:* running vivas for even 10% of a 300-person lecture course means roughly 30 oral exams per term with no rubric training provided, so grading became inconsistent examiner-to-examiner; faculty quietly stopped flagging suspected AI-written take-home work because misconduct hearings still leaned on AI-detector output as evidence and detector unreliability (GT-2) made hearings unwinnable, so referrals dropped even though the underlying behavior did not; large intro courses reverted the secured component to a light-weight "attendance quiz" rather than a real load-bearing exam, because writing and grading real secured content is unfunded extra labor.

*Student:* students discovered via shared forums which departments actually enforce viva sampling and which do not, and self-selected or complained their way into the lax ones; students used AI to pre-generate likely defense questions and answers from their own take-home essay before the viva, turning it into a memorization exercise rather than a genuine comprehension check; non-native-English and disabled students report the viva itself, not just the written exam, became their primary source of assessment anxiety, and the "accommodations built in from the start" promised by the policy were in practice a generic extended-time offer that did not address oral-communication-specific anxiety.

*Rival/vendor:* an ed-tech vendor released a real-time "interview coach" AI tool marketed for oral exams and interviews, delivered discreetly via earpiece or glasses-based display, within the three-year window; a competing university marketed "no oral defense required" as a selling point to prospective students who find vivas stressful, creating enrollment-driven pressure to water down the feature that gives the hybrid its integrity value.

**Clusters:**

- **Cluster 1 — Weight/load-bearing erosion** (administrator cause 1; instructor cause 3). Bears on: C4, A9. Triage: **Fatal** — directly falsifies must-have M1 the trade-off winner depends on. Tripwire: registrar tracks the secured component's % of final grade per department per term; two consecutive terms below a stated floor (e.g. 25%) fires. Owner: Associate Provost for Academic Affairs, reviewed at grade-submission audit. **Disposition — plan change:** write the minimum secured-component grade weight into institutional assessment policy itself, not left to department discretion.
- **Cluster 2 — Unfunded implementation drift** (administrator causes 2-3; instructor causes 1-3). Bears on: C4, C5 (step 2), A11, A12. Verification that would remove this cause: a direct replication of GT-1's design across other disciplines and institutions.

105	
106	**What was tried:** Considered under assumption A1/A7 — keep take-home assessment, require submissions to clear an AI-detection tool as the safeguard against undetected substitution.
107	
108	**Why abandoned:** GT-2 shows detectors are both statistically unreliable and specifically biased against non-native English speakers (61.22% average false-positive rate), and detector vendors are in an active, acknowledged arms race against paraphrasing/"humanizer" tools built specifically to defeat them (Turnitin's AIR-1 deployment). 109	
110	**What it ruled out:** Any recommendation of the form "keep take-home, but require AI-detector clearance" as a sufficient standalone integrity mechanism (chain C1).

112	### Dead End: Wait for better AI detectors before changing anything
113	
114	**What was tried:** Considered treating detector-improvement timelines as a legitimate basis for deferring any decision — i.e., "do nothing yet."
115	
116	**Why abandoned:** This is not actually a neutral no-cost choice. 126	**What it ruled out:** Answering the original question as posed with a simple "yes, replace" (see trade-off process output, Options/knockout).

55	### Conclusion C1: Detector-gated take-home assessment is not a working integrity safeguard today
56	
57	GT-1 (94% of AI take-home submissions undetected, real-world blind study) + GT-2 (61.22% average false-positive rate on non-native-English writing across 7 detectors)
58	→ even where a university requires AI-detector screening on take-home submissions as its integrity control, the tool that control relies on fails to catch the large majority of genuinely AI-written unsupervised submissions
59	→ the same detection tool simultaneously misflags a large share of genuine non-native-English student writing as AI-written
60	→ detector-gated take-home assessment is not a working safeguard, because it lets most AI-generated work through while wrongly threatening a specific subgroup of honest students — it cannot be the mechanism that makes take-home integrity-equivalent to a timed exam
61	
62	**Pre-check:** head GT-1, GT-2 · ?-marked: none · lowest cited: none · Inputs ceiling: HIGH
63	**Confidence:** HIGH — both inputs are read-at-source with named locations, the hop is a direct combination of two independently measured figures, and the live rival ("wait for better detectors to close the gap") is settled in Abandoned Reasoning: the bias is structural (worst against the exact population screening must not falsely accuse) and detectors face purpose-built evasion tools, so nothing in this analysis supports the gap closing on the timescale a current policy decision must be made on.
64	
65	### Conclusion C2: The AI-substitution problem already extends beyond take-home's current share of assessment, and is largely invisible
66	
67	C1 (detector-gating doesn't work) + GT-3 (88% of surveyed students used GenAI on assessed work in 2025; 18% pasted AI text directly in)
68	→ the practical AI-usage rate on assessed work today is already high under current mixed timed/take-home regimes
69	→ the one safeguard institutions lean on for take-home-specific integrity — detection — is shown non-functional by C1
70	→ converting the remaining timed-exam share of assessment to take-home format, with no substitute integrity mechanism, would extend the already-high and currently largely undetectable AI-substitution rate to the entire assessment portfolio, not just the take-home fraction [Assumes: A17]
71	
72	**Pre-check:** head C1 (HIGH), GT-3 · ?-marked: none · lowest cited: HIGH · Inputs ceiling: HIGH
73	**Confidence:** MEDIUM — Inputs and the direct hop are clean, but two things keep this below HIGH: (1) the 88% figure is a weak proxy for *prohibited* substitution specifically (most of it is likely disclosed/permitted use); the tighter 18% direct-inclusion figure partially, not fully, mitigates this; (2) a live rival is not settled: GT-1's 94%-undetected finding is drawn from five psychology modules at one UK university, and generalizing it to "any university's full course portfolio," including quantitative/technical disciplines where AI text is more checkable against shown work, rests on unverified assumption A17. Verification that would remove this cause: a direct replication of GT-1's design across other disciplines and institutions.
74	
75	### Conclusion C3: Timed, closed-resource recall assessment has pedagogical value that pure take-home replacement would forfeit
76	
77	GT-5? (retrieval practice ~2.5x retention benefit vs. restudying)
78	→ the durable-retention benefit reported in this literature is produced specifically by recalling under constraint (closed-resource, time-bounded) [Assumes: A14]
79	→ open-resource take-home work does not reproduce that constraint, more closely resembling the weaker "restudying with reference" condition in the same body of research
80	→ eliminating all closed-resource, time-bounded recall assessment removes a distinct pedagogical mechanism, not merely a redundant or inferior alternative to take-home work — so "take-home is strictly better pedagogy" is not supported as a blanket claim
81	
82	**Pre-check:** head GT-5? · ?-marked: GT-5? · lowest cited: none · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
83	**Confidence:** MEDIUM — GT-5? is unverified (reported-by-delegate); the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade is locating and reading a primary meta-analysis (e.g., the Roediger/Karpicke-line testing-effect literature) directly rather than relying on a search-engine summary. Additionally, hop 1 rests on the stated premise A14 (closed-resource condition specifically drives the benefit); the chain is unaffected in direction if A14 fails narrowly, since even a weaker "assessment format affects the retention mechanism at all" reading still supports the conclusion that removing all closed-resource recall is not neutral — but the *size* of the forfeited benefit would be smaller than GT-5?'s headline figure suggests. A rival not settled here: take-home work could in principle involve genuine self-testing regardless of format, which would weaken this chain's practical import; nothing in this analysis rules that rival out.
84	
85	### Conclusion C4: A hybrid model — not full replacement, not an unchanged status quo — is the recommended assessment format
86	
87	GT-1 (94% AI-undetected on take-home) + GT-5? (retrieval-practice benefit) + GT-7 (sampled-viva proposal, accommodation-inclusive) + GT-8? (equity/anxiety evidence, mixed) + C1 (detector-gating doesn't work)
88	→ a locked, weighted trade-off across Integrity, Pedagogical value, Authentic-task fit, Equity, Feasibility, and AI-resilience gives the hybrid (Option C) a total of 81 against the pure-timed-exam status quo (Option B) at 76, a margin of 5 driven mainly by Equity (+8) and Authentic-task fit (+6), partly offset by Feasibility (−6) and Pedagogical value (−3) [Assumes: A15]
89	→ full take-home replacement (Option A) was already knocked out on the Integrity must-have by C1 and GT-1/GT-2 directly, before this weighted comparison between Option B and Option C was run
90	→ the hybrid model is the recommended assessment format, conditional on its secured/timed component remaining genuinely grade-load-bearing and its accommodations being designed in from rollout
91	→ this recommendation is neither the pure take-home replacement the original question named nor an unmodified pure-timed-exam status quo
92	
93	**Pre-check:** head GT-1, GT-5?, GT-7, GT-8?, C1 (HIGH) · ?-marked: GT-5?, GT-8? · lowest cited: HIGH · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
94	**Confidence:** MEDIUM — capped by GT-5? and GT-8?, both unverified. Verification that would remove GT-5? as a cause: locating and reading a primary retrieval-practice meta-analysis directly (as C3 also notes). Verification that would remove GT-8? as a cause: locating and reading a primary accommodation-efficacy study directly (e.g., the Queen's University or Plymouth-hosted paper surfaced in search but not opened). The flip test recorded in the trade-off process output shows the result is sensitive specifically to the Equity criterion's weight — the one criterion resting on GT-8? — so this is the chain's named weakest link, not a generic hedge. Rival: the strongest competing conclusion is "Option B, pure timed-exam status quo, is the safer choice, since it wins if Equity is weighted down and does not depend on the hybrid's unverified implementation preconditions (A9-A13) actually holding." This rival is not fully settled — only an extreme (weight 4→1) devaluation of Equity flips the trade-off, but the implementation-precondition risk it points to is real and independently confirmed by the pre-mortem below (Clusters 1-2), which is why this chain is rated MEDIUM rather than HIGH.
95	
96	### Conclusion C5: The hybrid's integrity property is durable only under specific design and resourcing conditions, and is time-bound
97	
98	C4 (hybrid recommended, MEDIUM)
99	→[2nd] students facing unpredictable viva sampling have an incentive to shift take-home study behavior toward genuine comprehension rather than polished-but-unexamined output, partially restoring the retrieval-practice-like benefit C3 shows pure take-home would otherwise forfeit [Assumes: A16]
100	→[2nd] without dedicated, protected resourcing, faculty face a structural incentive to under-implement viva sampling and secured-component rigor over time, quietly reverting the hybrid toward a pure take-home model in practice even where its design is sound on paper
101	→[3rd] any layer of the hybrid that still leans on AI-text detectors rather than on the secured/timed component and the unpredictable viva for its integrity property remains exposed to the same detector-vendor arms race that defeats full replacement (Option A) under C1
102	→[3rd] the hybrid's integrity property must therefore be designed to rest only on the load-bearing secured component and the viva, never on detection
103	→[3rd] over a multi-year horizon, continuing growth in AI capability documented by GT-1 and GT-4 is plausibly extended from written artifacts to real-time conversational coaching during oral defense, which would erode the viva's own integrity value on a similar timescale to how detection lost its value against written text [Assumes: A13]

content.content:
1	## Answer
2	
3	**Recommendation:** Do not fully replace timed exams with take-home assessments, and do not leave the pure-timed-exam status quo unchanged either — adopt a hybrid: a grade-load-bearing secured/timed component, take-home format for extended/authentic tasks, and an unpredictable, accommodation-inclusive sampled oral defense, with its integrity resting on the secured component and the viva, never on AI-text detection (chain C4).
4	
5	**Band (from §6):** MEDIUM.
6	
7	**Would change it:** A primary-source read of the retrieval-practice and accommodation-efficacy literature (chain C4); institution-specific evidence that viva-sampling or secured-component resourcing cannot be sustained (chain C5); or evidence that real-time AI coaching capable of defeating live oral defense has emerged (chain C5).
8	
9	## 1. Problem Essence
10	
11	**Core problem:** Given that generative AI can now produce unsupervised written work that is largely undetectable and often graded higher than genuine student writing, does replacing timed, invigilated written exams with take-home assessments preserve — or degrade — a university's ability to certify that a student's degree reflects that student's own demonstrated competence, and is there a format allocation that does better than either named option alone?
12	
13	**Success criteria:**
14	1. The recommendation states, for each named option (timed-exam-only, take-home-only, and any hybrid/composite), whether it preserves the link between the credential and the individual student's own demonstrated competence, given current (2026) AI writing capability and current (2026) AI-detection reliability.
15	2. The recommendation names the specific assessment format(s) assigned to each of the competing goods this decision must balance — integrity/certification validity, retention/pedagogical value, authentic-task representativeness, and equity/accessibility — rather than declaring one goal an unconditional winner over the others.
16	3. The recommendation states an observable condition under which the recommended format mix would change (a falsification / "would change it" condition), so the answer is not a permanent verdict dressed as a first-principles conclusion.
17	
18	## 2. Assumptions Table
19	
20	| Assumption | Type | Treatment | Verdict | Verification |
21	|---|---|---|---|---|
22	| A1: AI-text detectors can reliably distinguish AI-written from student-written text, so a take-home model can be safeguarded by requiring detector clearance | untested belief | verify or flag unverified | Discard — contradicted directly by GT-2 (61.22% average false-positive rate on non-native-English writing) and by detector vendors' own admission of an active arms race against paraphrasing/"humanizer" tools (Turnitin AIR-1) | GT-2, read at source |
23	| A2: timed, invigilated written exams test only rote memorization and have no independent pedagogical value once resource-rich "authentic" tasks are available | convention | explicitly challenge before use | Challenge — retrieval-practice literature (GT-5?) indicates a distinct, durable retention benefit tied to closed-resource recall, not merely an inferior version of take-home work | GT-5?, unverified — flagged |
24	| A3: students mostly will not use AI on unsupervised take-home work if simply instructed not to (honor-code sufficiency) | untested belief | verify or flag unverified | Discard — contradicted by GT-3 (88% of surveyed UK undergraduates used GenAI on assessed work in 2025; 18% pasted AI text directly in) and GT-6? (contract-cheating rates rising, take-home/unsupervised format specifically implicated) | GT-3, read at source; GT-6?, unverified — flagged |
25	| A4: removing timed exams is a pure equity improvement with no offsetting equity cost | convention | explicitly challenge before use | Challenge — GT-8? shows a mixed picture: timed conditions are a real anxiety trigger for some students, but unsupervised take-home formats carry their own inequities (home-environment disparity, GT-2's bias against non-native English writers under any detector-based enforcement) | GT-8?, unverified — flagged |
26	| A5: a university can feasibly add a secured, timed or live-proctored component to every assessment at scale without prohibitive cost | current constraint | record expiry conditions | Accept — expires (partially) once scalable, validated AI-assisted oral-assessment grading tools exist; today, full invigilation of everything is not feasible, but *sampled* proctoring/oral defense (GT-7) is | GT-7, read at source, for the sampling proposal; the AI-assisted-grading claim itself unverified — flagged |
27	| A6: LLM writing capability is limited to short-form or generic content and will not extend to discipline-specific, professional-level unsupervised writing tasks | untested belief | verify or flag unverified | Discard — GT-4 shows GPT-4 passing a professional bar exam (68th-90th percentile) including full essay and performance-test components, i.e., capability already spans complex, professional-level written and applied-reasoning tasks | GT-4, read at source |
28	| A7: AI-detector unreliability is a temporary engineering problem, so a university should wait for better detectors rather than redesign assessment now | convention | explicitly challenge before use | Challenge — the bias is structural (worst precisely against the population a university must not wrongly accuse) and detectors face active, purpose-built evasion tools (paraphrasers/"humanizers"), so overall accuracy improving would not by itself close the equity/evidentiary problem | GT-2, read at source, for the bias finding; the arms-race dynamic reported-by-delegate — unverified — flagged |
29	| A8: a hybrid model's sampled oral-defense (viva) component is procedurally fair only if disability/anxiety/language accommodations are designed in from the outset, not bolted on afterward | current constraint | record expiry conditions | Accept — expires only if/when a validated inclusive-by-default oral-assessment protocol exists; until then this is a non-negotiable design requirement, not an optional add-on | GT-7, read at source (the cited proposal states this condition explicitly) |
30	| A9 (surfaced via Phase 2 inversion, precondition P1): a hybrid model's secured/timed component retains a grade weight high enough to be load-bearing (cannot be compensated away by take-home performance) over time | untested belief | verify or flag unverified | Accept — flagged; this is a design requirement whose failure is the single most-cited pre-mortem risk (Cluster 1) | unverified — flagged; no institution-specific evidence available to this analysis |
31	| A10 (inversion precondition P2): the viva-sampling mechanism remains unpredictable to students (not pre-announced or self-selectable) | untested belief | verify or flag unverified | Accept — flagged; failure here is pre-mortem Cluster 3's "gaming the known mechanism" risk | unverified — flagged |
32	| A11 (inversion precondition P3): institutional resourcing for faculty time (viva administration, secured-exam design/grading) persists beyond the initial policy rollout | current constraint | record expiry conditions | Accept — expires if a dedicated, protected budget line is written into the rollout plan rather than drawn from existing TA/faculty hours; absent that, this is pre-mortem Cluster 2's central risk | unverified — flagged; institution-specific |
33	| A12 (inversion precondition P4): oral-defense (viva) grading is reliable and consistent across examiners | untested belief | verify or flag unverified | Challenge — a specific reliability figure (Cronbach's α ≈ 0.75-0.80 for structured oral formats) surfaced in initial search results but could not be confirmed by opening the cited source directly; treated as unverified rather than used as a ground truth | unverified — flagged; source not confirmed on direct read attempt |
34	| A13 (inversion precondition P6): live, real-time AI assistance during an oral defense can be prevented or detected for the years the hybrid model is expected to remain standard | current constraint | record expiry conditions | Challenge — no ground truth in this analysis establishes this is currently happening at scale, but the capability trend documented in GT-1/GT-4 makes it a foreseeable medium-term threat to the viva's own integrity value | unverified — flagged; forward-looking, no direct evidence either way |
35	| A14 (surfaced Phase 4, chain C3): the closed-resource recall condition specifically — not "assessment occurring" in general — is what drives the testing-effect/retrieval-practice benefit, so take-home format does not reproduce it | untested belief | verify or flag unverified | Accept — flagged; a plausible reading of the retrieval-practice literature summary (GT-5?) but not independently confirmed at the primary source | unverified — flagged |
36	| A15 (surfaced Phase 4, chain C4): the six locked trade-off criteria (integrity, pedagogical value, authentic-task fit, equity, feasibility, AI-resilience) are jointly sufficient, with no material seventh criterion omitted | untested belief | verify or flag unverified | Accept — flagged; criteria were derived from the Phase 2 fishbone's six-category sweep (People, Process, Technology, Environment, Information, Resources), which gives reasonable but not exhaustive coverage | unverified — flagged; scope limit of this analysis |
37	| A16 (surfaced Phase 4, chain C5): students respond as rational, incentive-sensitive actors to the sampled-viva mechanism, rather than discounting a low-probability risk and ignoring it | untested belief | verify or flag unverified | Accept — flagged; behavioral-economics literature on low-probability-risk discounting suggests this is not guaranteed, which is exactly why pre-mortem Cluster 3 treats gaming as a live, not merely hypothetical, risk | unverified — flagged |
38	| A17 (surfaced Phase 4, chain C2): findings drawn primarily from UK higher-education contexts (GT-1, GT-3, GT-7) generalize to other national/institutional contexts | untested belief | verify or flag unverified | Accept — flagged; treated as a live rival to C2 rather than settled, since no ground truth in this analysis establishes cross-national generalization | unverified — flagged |
39	
40	## 3. Ground Truths
41	
42	- **GT-1** In a blind study, GPT-4-generated submissions were injected into unsupervised, window-timed take-home exams across five undergraduate psychology modules at a UK university (Short Answer Questions: 2.5-hour window, 200-word answers; essays: 8-hour window, 1,500 words). 94% of the AI submissions went undetected by examiners (97% under stricter criteria requiring explicit mention of AI); AI submissions scored on average half a grade boundary higher than real students; there was an 83.4% chance that AI submissions on a given module would outperform a random selection of real student submissions of the same size. — source: Scarfe, Watcham, Clarke & Roesch, "A real-world test of artificial intelligence infiltration of a university examinations system: A 'Turing Test' case study," *PLOS ONE*, 2024; read-at-source: full text, PMC11206930, Results/Discussion sections (figures quoted directly).
43	- **GT-2** Across seven widely used AI-text detectors tested on 91 TOEFL essays written by non-native English speakers, the average false-positive rate (genuine human writing flagged as AI-generated) was 61.22%; on 88 US 8th-grade essays by native English writers, the average false-positive rate was approximately 5.19%. — source: Liang, Yuksekgonul, Mao, Wu & Zou, published in *Patterns* (2023); read-at-source: arXiv:2304.02819v3, full text, Results section (figures quoted directly).
44	- **GT-3** In a survey of 1,041 UK undergraduates (fielded by Savanta), 88% reported using generative AI tools for assessments in 2025 (up from 53% in 2024); 18% reported including AI-generated text directly in submitted work; 76% believed their institution would detect AI use if it occurred. — source: HEPI/Kortext Student Generative AI Survey 2025; read-at-source: hepi.ac.uk release page, 2025-02-26 (figures quoted directly).
45	- **GT-4** GPT-4 scored approximately 297/400 on the Uniform Bar Exam, within the 68th-90th percentile of human test-takers depending on jurisdiction and exam administration; it scored 4.2/6.0 on both the Multistate Essay Examination and the Multistate Performance Test (a score of 4+ is generally passing); it scored 75.7% on the multiple-choice component, exceeding the average human test-taker by more than 7 points. — source: Katz, Bommarito, Gao & Arredondo, "GPT-4 Passes the Bar Exam," published study; read-at-source: full text, PMC10894685 (figures quoted directly).
46	- **GT-5?** Retrieval-practice/testing-effect meta-analytic literature reports that information retrieved under recall/test conditions is recalled on subsequent tests roughly 2.5x more often than information reviewed via restudying, with benefits persisting over weeks to years and replicated across ages and content domains. — cited to: multiple meta-analyses summarized in web-search results (e.g., work associated with Roediger/Karpicke-line testing-effect research); reported-by-delegate: search-engine summary; cited sources not opened by this analysis.
47	- **GT-6?** Contract-cheating prevalence research reports self-reported contract cheating rising from a historic average of approximately 3.5% to approximately 15.7% in samples from 2014 onward; unsupervised/take-home assessment format is specifically named in this literature as expanding opportunities for collusion or outsourcing; one cited institution (UNSW) saw detected cheating rates roughly double post-COVID (approximately 2% to approximately 4.5%), coinciding with expanded remote/take-home assessment. — cited to: Newton-line meta-analytic literature, *Frontiers in Education* and related sources; reported-by-delegate: search-engine summary; cited sources not opened by this analysis.
48	- **GT-7** A proposal for randomly sampling approximately 10% of students per assessment for a short oral defense (viva), as a scalable integrity/comprehension check layered onto existing quality-assurance processes, explicitly conditioned on building in "clear guidelines for extenuating circumstances and reasonable adjustments" for disability, anxiety, and language barriers from the outset. — source: "Sampled vivas are pivotal in combating AI cheating," *Times Higher Education*; read-at-source: full article text, timeshighereducation.com/node/735603 (proposal and conditions quoted/paraphrased directly from the fetched text).
49	- **GT-8?** Test-anxiety/disability-accommodation research indicates extended time is the most frequently requested and granted postsecondary testing accommodation, and that timed conditions are commonly cited as the primary anxiety trigger for test-anxious students; however, some studies report no significant difference in timed-task performance between students clinically diagnosed with anxiety/depression and controls, and equity researchers argue reactive, case-by-case accommodation does not by itself produce equitable outcomes at scale, recommending inclusive-by-default assessment design as a complement. — cited to: multiple sources summarized in web-search results (e.g., work hosted via Queen's University and Plymouth-affiliated repositories); reported-by-delegate: search-engine summary; cited sources not opened by this analysis.
50	
51	**Provenance summary:**
52	```text
53	?-marked: GT-5, GT-6, GT-8 (3 of 8)
54	Read-at-source: GT-1 — PMC11206930 full text, Results/Discussion
55	Read-at-source: GT-2 — arXiv:2304.02819v3 full text, Results
56	Read-at-source: GT-3 — hepi.ac.uk release page, 2025-02-26
57	Read-at-source: GT-4 — PMC10894685 full text
58	Read-at-source: GT-7 — timeshighereducation.com/node/735603 full text
59	```
60	
61	## 4. Derivation Chains
62	
63	### Conclusion C1: Detector-gated take-home assessment is not a working integrity safeguard today
64	
65	GT-1 (94% of AI take-home submissions undetected, real-world blind study) + GT-2 (61.22% average false-positive rate on non-native-English writing across 7 detectors)
66	→ even where a university requires AI-detector screening on take-home submissions as its integrity control, the tool that control relies on fails to catch the large majority of genuinely AI-written unsupervised submissions
67	→ the same detection tool simultaneously misflags a large share of genuine non-native-English student writing as AI-written
68	→ detector-gated take-home assessment is not a working safeguard, because it lets most AI-generated work through while wrongly threatening a specific subgroup of honest students — it cannot be the mechanism that makes take-home integrity-equivalent to a timed exam
69	
70	**Pre-check:** head GT-1, GT-2 · ?-marked: none · lowest cited: none · Inputs ceiling: HIGH
71	**Confidence:** HIGH — both inputs are read-at-source with named locations, the hop is a direct combination of two independently measured figures, and the live rival ("wait for better detectors to close the gap") is settled in Abandoned Reasoning: the bias is structural (worst against the exact population screening must not falsely accuse) and detectors face purpose-built evasion tools, so nothing in this analysis supports the gap closing on the timescale a current policy decision must be made on.
72	
73	### Conclusion C2: The AI-substitution problem already extends beyond take-home's current share of assessment, and is largely invisible
74	
75	C1 (detector-gating doesn't work) + GT-3 (88% of surveyed students used GenAI on assessed work in 2025; 18% pasted AI text directly in)
76	→ the practical AI-usage rate on assessed work today is already high under current mixed timed/take-home regimes
77	→ the one safeguard institutions lean on for take-home-specific integrity — detection — is shown non-functional by C1
78	→ converting the remaining timed-exam share of assessment to take-home format, with no substitute integrity mechanism, would extend the already-high and currently largely undetectable AI-substitution rate to the entire assessment portfolio, not just the take-home fraction [Assumes: A17]
79	
80	**Pre-check:** head C1 (HIGH), GT-3 · ?-marked: none · lowest cited: HIGH · Inputs ceiling: HIGH
81	**Confidence:** MEDIUM — Inputs and the direct hop are clean, but two things keep this below HIGH: (1) the 88% figure is a weak proxy for *prohibited* substitution specifically (most of it is likely disclosed/permitted use); the tighter 18% direct-inclusion figure partially, not fully, mitigates this; (2) a live rival is not settled: GT-1's 94%-undetected finding is drawn from five psychology modules at one UK university, and generalizing it to "any university's full course portfolio," including quantitative/technical disciplines where AI text is more checkable against shown work, rests on unverified assumption A17. 167	## 6. Conclusion
168	
169	**Recommended approach:** Do not replace timed exams outright with take-home assessments, and do not leave the pre-AI timed-exam-only status quo unchanged either — adopt a hybrid model: a grade-load-bearing secured/timed (invigilated or live-proctored) component, take-home format reserved for extended/authentic tasks, and an unpredictable, accommodation-inclusive, randomly sampled (~10%) oral defense layered on take-home submissions, with its integrity property deliberately designed to rest on the secured component and the viva rather than on AI-text detection (chain C4, chain C1).
170	
171	**Key insight:** The intuitive framing of this decision as "timed exams vs. take-home" hides the fact that the safeguard most people assume would make take-home safe — AI-detection software — is not merely imperfect but measurably non-functional today, and fails worst against exactly the population (non-native English writers) it would be most damaging to wrongly accuse; a real-world blind study additionally shows the substitution problem is not hypothetical but already occurring undetected at a 94% rate in precisely this assessment format (chain C1, chain C2, chain C6).
172	
173	**Trade-offs acknowledged:** The hybrid model does not deliver the retrieval-practice/retention benefit of an all-timed-exam regime at full strength (chain C3, chain C4 — Pedagogical value scored 4 vs. Option B's 5), and it costs more faculty time than either pure option, with its equity and integrity benefits conditional on real resourcing and design discipline that this analysis cannot verify any specific institution will actually deliver — no chain — flagged assumption only for the institution-specific claim that resourcing will in fact be sustained, since that lies outside this analysis's evidence base (chain C5 names the resourcing and design risks generally).

Chain C1 (HIGH) and chain C2 (MEDIUM) establish the problem the recommendation responds to with higher confidence than the recommendation's own optimality; the weighted trade-off's margin (5 points) is real but not large, and the flip test shows it is sensitive specifically to the Equity criterion, whose factual basis (GT-8?) is unverified. Chain C1: rival "detector output could still be used as one input among several for human review, rather than discarded entirely" — rival not applicable — this is a refinement of C1's conclusion (detectors cannot be *the* safeguard), not a competing claim C1 must rule out. Chain C2: rival ("88% mostly reflects permitted use") is addressed and only partially settled on C2's own confidence line (MEDIUM), which the Rivals axis here points back to rather than re-arguing. 289	
290	**Premise.** It is now three years since [this university] adopted the hybrid assessment model. The policy has failed — certification validity has not been restored, and the university faces a fresh integrity crisis, this time with less credibility to fix it because it already claimed to have solved the problem once.

292	**Causes** (unfiltered, from four viewpoints — administrator, instructor, student, rival/vendor):

294	*Administrator:* the secured/timed component's grade weight was negotiated down department-by-department until it was no longer load-bearing in several majors; no central budget line was created for viva administration, so it was funded out of existing TA hours that evaporated within two years; the "10% random sample" became "10% of whichever students show up to office hours," a self-selection bias defeating the design.
295	
296	*Instructor:* running vivas for even 10% of a 300-person lecture course means roughly 30 oral exams per term with no rubric training provided, so grading became inconsistent examiner-to-examiner; faculty quietly stopped flagging suspected AI-written take-home work because misconduct hearings still leaned on AI-detector output as evidence and detector unreliability (GT-2) made hearings unwinnable, so referrals dropped even though the underlying behavior did not; large intro courses reverted the secured component to a light-weight "attendance quiz" rather than a real load-bearing exam, because writing and grading real secured content is unfunded extra labor.
297	
298	*Student:* students discovered via shared forums which departments actually enforce viva sampling and which do not, and self-selected or complained their way into the lax ones; students used AI to pre-generate likely defense questions and answers from their own take-home essay before the viva, turning it into a memorization exercise rather than a genuine comprehension check; non-native-English and disabled students report the viva itself, not just the written exam, became their primary source of assessment anxiety, and the "accommodations built in from the start" promised by the policy were in practice a generic extended-time offer that did not address oral-communication-specific anxiety.

300	*Rival/vendor:* an ed-tech vendor released a real-time "interview coach" AI tool marketed for oral exams and interviews, delivered discreetly via earpiece or glasses-based display, within the three-year window; a competing university marketed "no oral defense required" as a selling point to prospective students who find vivas stressful, creating enrollment-driven pressure to water down the feature that gives the hybrid its integrity value.

Tripwire: registrar tracks the secured component's % of final grade per department per term; two consecutive terms below a stated floor (e.g. 25%) fires. Owner: Associate Provost for Academic Affairs, reviewed at grade-submission audit. **Disposition — plan change:** write the minimum secured-component grade weight into institutional assessment policy itself, not left to department discretion.

Tripwire: annual audit of planned (10%) vs. actually-administered viva rate per course, plus an inter-rater spot-check on a sample of vivas. Owner: Teaching & Learning office, published annually. **Disposition — plan change:** rollout budget must include dedicated, protected staffing for viva administration and secured-exam design, sized to enrollment and approved before rollout, not requested after a shortfall appears.
306	- **Cluster 3 — Gaming the known mechanism** (student causes 1-2). Bears on: C4, C5 (step 1), A10, A16. Triage: **Costly but survivable** — a viva reduced to "defend memorized talking points" still requires engagement with the material, partially preserving C5's first-hop benefit even as a weaker check than intended. Tripwire: track the gap between take-home submission quality and viva performance over time; a widening gap while written-work quality keeps rising signals disconnection. Owner: department assessment committees, reviewed each term. **Disposition — accepted risk with named mitigation:** rotate/randomize viva question framing each term to defeat pre-generated answer banks; keep sampling genuinely unpredictable (post-submission selection, never pre-announced).
307	- **Cluster 4 — Oral defense itself becomes AI-assistable** (rival/vendor cause 1). Bears on: C5 (step 4), A13, GT-1/GT-4's capability trend. 308	- **Cluster 5 — Enrollment-competitive pressure to weaken the viva** (rival/vendor cause 2). Bears on: C4 (Feasibility/Equity trade-off), Cluster 1. Tripwire: admissions/program-review data showing applicants citing assessment format as a reason for choosing a competitor. Owner: Admissions/Provost office, reviewed annually. **Disposition — accepted risk with named mitigation:** position the secured/oral components explicitly as credential-value protection in communications to prospective students and employers, rather than assuming competitive pressure will not materialize.
309	
310	**Falsification.** The hybrid recommendation (chain C4) is false — i.e., should not have been adopted over the pure-timed-exam status quo — if, within the first 2-3 years of implementation, the secured component's grade weight is not sustained at a load-bearing level across most departments (Cluster 1's tripwire fires) **and** the viva-sampling mechanism is not actually administered at its designed rate (Cluster 2's tripwire fires) at the same time; under that joint condition the hybrid reduces to Option A (pure take-home) in practice while carrying Option C's extra cost, a configuration no chain in this analysis evaluated or supports.
